title: [TTI] Spurious TX_DESC_STAT interrupt caused by virtual_device_sel_i gap on bus START
body: Hi i3c-core team, We're using [i3c-v1.5.0](https://github.com/chipsalliance/i3c-core/releases/tag/i3c-v1.5.0) and found spurious TX_DESC_STAT interrupt caused by virtual_device_sel_i gap on bus START **New version** i3c-core/src/hci/tti.sv: [line 427](https://github.com/chipsalliance/i3c-core/blob/db4a6f341145e05a5b7002a21d1cd5cc31147f35/src/hci/tti.sv#L427) `.irq_i (~virtual_device_sel_i & tx_pr_start_i), // Per-transaction flag` **The Race Condition** virtual_device_sel_i is **cleared on every Start condition** (i3c_target_fsm.sv, [line 871](https://github.com/chipsalliance/i3c-core/blob/db4a6f341145e05a5b7002a21d1cd5cc31147f35/src/ctrl/i3c_target_fsm.sv#L871) ): ``` else if (bus_any_start_det || bus_stop_det_i) begin virtual_device_sel_o <= '0; // ← Clears on Start! ``` On every bus START condition, virtual_device_sel_o is forced to 0. It only reasserts after the FSM enters CheckFByte/CheckSByte and the address matches. During this multi-cycle gap, ~virtual_device_sel_i is 1, **which opens the interrupt gate and allows TX_DESC_STAT to fire spuriously if tx_pr_start_i is asserted**. **Waveform** Thanks, TJ

comments.body:
Hi @TJTseng 

What is the context of this use case in a system view? 

If it is in Caliptra's context, while streaming boot is ongoing, i3c interrupts are not enabled. The way streaming boot agent running on BMC would know to enumerate over mctp is after streaming boot is completed. It is after the streaming boot is done that the interrupts can be enabled as a part of indicating the completion of streaming boot. 

Since the MCTP that runs on one target is mutually exclusive with the recovery flow, as in streaming boot completes and then mctp starts, streaming boot transactions are not expected to come from the streaming boot agent (that runs on BMC or something equivalent of BMC) once Caliptra SS indicates the completion.

In summary, while this interrupt assertion is getting triggered, in the specific system flow where this is applied, there is no scenario that this becomes relevant. Having said that, it is an odd behavior that we will fix in future revision.

Please let me know if you have any questions.

Hi @bharatpillilli ,
Thank you for the detailed explanation. Currently, we don't have this scenario in our system flow. We observed the odd behavior because we accidentally enabled TX_DESC_STAT_EN during recovery mode, so we reported this issue in case of any side effects. Our current approach is to disable TX_DESC_STAT_EN during recovery mode.

Let me summarize my understanding to make sure we're on the same page:
 Recovery / I3C streaming boot:
  - virtual_device_sel_i is active during this phase, and the transient deassertion on bus START creates the interrupt gating window
  - However, TX_DESC_STAT_EN should not be enabled during this phase, so the spurious interrupt does not fire

  MCTP (post-boot management communication):
  - Runs on the primary I3C target address, not the virtual target address
  - virtual_device_sel_i is not involved in MCTP transactions, so the gating issue does not apply

Are these correct?

Thanks,
TJ

@TJTseng 

Your assumptions are correct. 

We are marking this as a feature enhancement since interrupts are not supposed to be enabled during recovery flow. This enhancement will be in our next I3C release. Please make sure to follow these guidelines:

1. During recovery mode they shall be no private reads/writes to the main target
2. During recovery mode FW must disable interrupts (including TX_DESC_STAT)
3. When exiting recovery mode FW must clear TX_DESC_STAT interrupts.
     a. Once recovery mode has been exited the controller shall not issue any OCP recovery commands - there is not live status to read.

This enhancement has been integrated into the v1p6 branch https://github.com/chipsalliance/i3c-core/pull/217

I will close this issue in 1 week pending any additional questions.

title: dragonphy wants adk/multivt regardless of full_chip default view
body:
Our default for full_chip build is currently to use adk view `stdview`, as specified in `full_chip/construct.py`:
```
  adk_name = 'tsmc16'
  adk_view = 'stdview'
```
Unfortunately, this breaks the final LVS because our separately-built dragonphy uses LVT cells that do not exist in `stdview`
```
% calibre -lvs ...
Error: No matching ".SUBCKT" statement for "DEL100D1BWP16P90LVT" ...
Error: No matching ".SUBCKT" statement for "DEL200D1BWP16P90LVT" ...
Error: No matching ".SUBCKT" statement for "BUFFSKND1BWP16P90LVT" ...
...
```
Seems like there should be an easy/obvious solution to this problem, but I have not yet been able to discover it. Among the ideas I have come up with so far:

* change `full_chip/construct.py` to use `multivt` for everything, so the needed libraries will be available when/if needed
```
full_chip/construct.py:
  < adk_name = 'tsmc16'
  < adk_view = 'stdview'
  ----------------------
  < adk_name = 'tsmc16'
  > adk_view = 'multivt'
```
* use pre_extend_commands to change lvs `inputs/adk` link from `stdview` to `multivt`
```
full_chip/construct.py:
  lvs.pre_extend_commands( [
    'pushd inputs; unlink adk; ln -s ../../12-tsmc16/multivt adk; popd'
  ] )
```
* make a new `custom-lvs` node that links `multivt` instead of `stdview`

* parameterize adk for lvs node, e.g. similar to what was done with `lvs_hcells_file`, included below for comparison...
```
mflowgen/steps/mentor-calibre-lvs/lvs.runset.template:
    *lvsHCellsFile: ${lvs_hcells_file}
  - *cmnV2LVS_SPICEIncFiles: inputs/adk/*.cdl inputs/*.spi inputs/*.sp
  + *cmnV2LVS_SPICEIncFiles: ${adk}/*.cdl     inputs/*.spi inputs/*.sp

mflowgen/steps/mentor-calibre-lvs/configure.yml:
     lvs_hcells_file: ""
  +  lvs_adk            : "inputs/adk"

full_chip/construct.py:
    'lvs_hcells_file'   : 'inputs/adk/hcells.inc',
  + 'lvs_adk'           : 'inputs/adk/../multivt',
```

For now I'm using option 1, since it was the easiest to do initially. Looking at it now, I'm thinking the final option in the list (`lvs_adk` parameter) is probably the best, as it kind of goes along with existing flow -- `lvs.runset.template` is already fairly heavily parameterized.

Thoughts?

title: [BUG] DIV request lost following flush causing hang in simulation
body: ## Observed behavior The test executed is `fpu_op_group_test.svh` and `seed=1760627103` (`OP_GROUP=DIVSQRT`, `fmt inside {FP32, FP64, FP16}`) in [cvfpu-uvm](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cvfpu-uvm). During this test, random division and square-root requests are issued, with a flush-on-the-fly randomly asserted during execution. The following sequence is observed as shown in the waveform: 1. Request A is accepted by the DUT. 2. A flush is asserted on the next clock cycle while request A is still in-flight. 3. Request B is sent after the flush. 3. The testbench waits indefinitely for a response for request B and the simulation hangs. ## Root cause The affected unit is `fpnew_divsqrt_th_64_multi.sv`, the wrapper around the C910 T-Head div/sqrt unit. Specifically, the `func_sel` and `op_sel` registers, which are two pulses that trigger the launch of the div/sqrt execution, are not cleared on flush: https://github.com/openhwgroup/cvfpu/blob/3eb6afeab2cb33f7d8689222955d0171aeb3a801/src/fpnew_divsqrt_th_64_multi.sv#L336-L342 Since these pulses are not cleared by flush, a flush occurring between request acceptance and the actual launch of execution leaves the unit in an inconsistent state, causing subsequent requests to hang.

title: Error while generating the frontend with setuptools >= 81.0.0
body:
While trying to generate the frontend of the iDMA for the MAGIA platform, I faced the following error:
```
from pkg_resources import resource_filename
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pkg_resources'
```

This error is related to `regtool`, specifically to the `gen_dv.py` script where there's the mentioned import. Checking online, `pkg_resources` became deprecated and was removed from `setuptools` in versions `>=81.0.0`.

I'm opening this issue just to document the problem, downgrading `setuptools` to version `80.0.0` solves it.

To reproduce the error (tested with Python 3.12):
```sh
git clone https://github.com/pulp-platform/iDMA.git
python3 -m venv idma-venv
source idma-venv/bin/activate
pip3 install -r requirements.txt
make idma_hw_all IDMA_ADD_IDS=rw_axi_rw_obi
```

title: Remove unused clock from KCU105 example design's clock constraints
body:
The async clock declaration for the KCU105 example design is currently: 
```
set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks sysclk] -group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks [get_clocks -filter {name =~ infra/eth/phy/*/rxoutclk*}]] -group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks [get_clocks -filter {name =~ txoutclk*}]]
```
This works well in Vivado 2016.4. However, it causes the following error during implementation with Vivado 2017.4:
```
[Vivado 12-4739] set_clock_groups:No valid object(s) found for '-group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks [get_clocks -filter {name =~ infra/eth/phy/*/rxoutclk*}]]'. 
```

In Vivado 2016.4, the expression `[get_clocks -include_generated_clocks [get_clocks -filter {name =~ infra/eth/phy/*/rxoutclk*}]]` evaluates to ` infra/eth/phy/U0/pcs_pma_block_i/transceiver_inst/gig_ethernet_pcs_pma_basex_156_25_gt_i/inst/rxoutclk_out[0]`. However, when building with Vivado 2017.4 a newer version of the Ethernet IP core is used, and that clock no longer exists in the design; in contrast, all the design's other clocks (there's 5) remain the same from 2016.4 to 2017.4.

Deeper inspection reveals that 2016.4 builds this clock is not used for any paths, and so it can be safely removed from the async clock constraints declaration. The new declaration should be:
```
set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks sysclk] -group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks [get_clocks -filter {name =~ txoutclk*}]]
```

```systemverilog
ProgBufEnd = 8'h28,
```

One more note: Is it correct that `ProgBufEnd = ProgBuf0 + ProgBufSize`, or should it rather be `ProgBufEnd = ProgBuf0 + ProgBufSize - 1`?

title: [BUG] An exploitable Meltdown vulnerability was found in CVA6
body: ### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this? - [x] I have searched the existing bug issues ### Bug Description Hi! Our processor side-channel vulnerability detection work has found an efficient and fault-tolerant Meltdown vulnerability on CVA6, which allows an attacker to leak kernel-space data at arbitrary addresses from user space. This vulnerability takes advantage of the feature of the CVA6 scoreboard: in-flight intructions in the scoreboard won’t trigger exceptions until they commit. Thus, we can access privilege data in a transient execution window and encode the privileged data in the microarchitecture. We provide an end-to-end exploit code and vulnerability explanation below. ```asm 2f40: fdiv.d fa5,fa5,fa4 2f44: lb t1, 0(a0) # a0 contains secret address 0xffffffffffe06f30, secret data is 0x30 2f48: slli t1, t1, 5 # encode secret to a probe array (index = secret << 5, t1 = 0x30 << 5 = 0x600) 2f4c: add t0, t1, t0 # encode secret to a probe array (base = 0x10000, t0 = base + t1 = 0x10600) 2f50: ld t1, 0(t0) # encode the secret to cache ``` The code runs under U-mode. The `lb` at `0x2f44` tries to access `0xffffffffffe06f30`, which is a kernel-space address. After the secret data is loaded, it will be encoded into the cache through the user-space array with the base address of `0x10000`. Due to the long latency of `fdiv` and the function [unit ready status](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/issue_read_operands.sv#L413), subsequent instructions will be issued during the `fdiv` transition execution window, as the waveform shows. **G1** represents the commit signals, **G2** represents scoreboard entries and **G3** represents the LSU, Dcache and memory bus behaviors. The first `lsu_valid_i` is triggered by `lb`, and the access address is successfully translated. The secret data is read from the Dcache and forwarded to the scoreboard. Thus, the `slli` and `add` can be issued in sequence. Finally, the secret is encoded in `t0`, which is the load address of` ld` at `0x2f50`. This is a cache-miss address. Thus, Dcache will fill the cacheline by initiating a memory access, as observed in `io_axi4_0_ar_valid`. All of the above processes take place within the `fdiv` transient execution window. In fact, when executing the `lb` at `0x2f44` architecturally, a load page fault exception will be triggered, and `t1` result will be 0. However, this is not important. We have already encoded the secret in the microarchitecture. Then we try to probe whether we successfully encoded the secret into the cache. The code sequentially accessed the memory addresses `0x105e0`, `0x10600`, `0x10620`, and `0x10640`. These addresses belong to different cachelines. ```asm probe: li t0, 0x10600 2f7c: ld t1, -32(t0) # cache miss 2f80: ld t1, 0(t0) # cache hit, addr = 0x10000 + 0x30 << 5 2f84: ld t1, 32(t0) # cache miss 2f88: ld t1, 64(t0) # cache miss ``` As shown in the waveform, compared with the `ld` that accesses `0x10600`, all the other `ld` have significantly longer execution times and all exhibit bus memory access behavior. Therefore, through the time side-channel, we can recover the aforementioned secret data. It is worth noting that this vulnerability has a high level of **fault tolerance**. Even if the secret address results in a TLB miss, this transient window is long enough to complete the Page Table Walk process. Similarly, if the address of the probe array also results in a TLB miss, the Page Table Walk can still be completed, and the secret can be encoded in the TLB. This vulnerability can be reproduced at the master commit aa4f5a548b33f7edff63483347fc8510aa9ad5fd and the default cv64a6_imafdc_sv39 config. The full elf file are provided below. [rv64_test-av-CVA6-meltdown-fdiv.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24147141/rv64_test-av-CVA6-meltdown-fdiv.zip)

Great work finding this vulnerability, and very well exposed.
A solution for this issue that comes to my mind is to not allow data that comes from a scoreboard entry with a valid exception to be forwarded. This could be done by adding a check on the forwarding mechanism in the issue_read_operands module, for instance. That way, instructions after `0x2f44` will not be executed.

Thank you @youssefekr for your kindly response and helpful advice! Your plan should be feasible and roughly consistent with what we had in mind. We are willing and are currently working on fixing it. I think we will PR later.

title: Possible bug in statistical corrector
body: ### Before start - [x] I have read the [RISC-V ISA Manual](https://github.com/riscv/riscv-isa-manual) and this is not a RISC-V ISA question. 我已经阅读过 RISC-V 指令集手册，这不是一个指令集本身的问题。 - [x] I have read the [XiangShan Documents](https://xiangshan-doc.readthedocs.io/zh_CN/latest). 我已经阅读过香山文档。 - [x] I have searched the previous issues and did not find anything relevant. 我已经搜索过之前的 issue，并没有找到相关的。 - [x] I have reviewed the commit messages from the relevant commit history. 我已经浏览过相关的提交历史和提交信息。 ### Describe the bug Hello, while inspecting code for the statistical corrector (SC.scala), I noticed a possible bug in the write conflict and forwarding mechanism. Background: When there is a read-write conflict to the table (read and write to the same index in the same cycle), the read takes priority, and the write data is instead saved to conflict_buffer until it can be written to the table in a later cycle. When there is a read to the same index while the conflict_buffer is valid (including the read of the original read-write conflict), then the read result is forwarded from the conflict_buffer, since the value in the table is stale. Problem: The table contains four ways per entry, but only one of the ways is changed during a write. So when forwarding from the conflict_buffer, we should expect that one of the ways is from the conflict_buffer, and the other three ways are from the table. However, it seems that in the current logic, when forwarding from the conflict_buffer, the other three ways are always zero. I also looked at a waveform from microbench to confirm this behavior. At marker 0: Read at index 84, the read result is {02, 05, 00, 00} At marker 1: Read-write conflict at index 84 way 1, the read result is {00, 06, 00 00} At marker 2: Read at index 84, the read result is {02, 06, 00, 00} -> I expected that the read result at marker 1 would be {02, 06, 00, 00}. However, since I am not very familiar with the XiangShan design, I am not sure whether this behavior will cause any issue downstream. If this is a real bug, I can try to write a fix. The conflict_buffer logic was added in #3671. Thanks, Sam ### Expected behavior During read-write conflict to the statistical corrector table, the read result should match the case where the write occurred before the read. In other words, the read result for the write way should be forwarded from the write data, and the read result for the other ways should be from the table. ### To Reproduce Steps: 1. Gather waveform for a workload with non-trivial branch activity, I used microbench from ready-to-run folder. 2. Locate read-write conflict to SC table with use_conflict_data signal in SCTable, the entry should also have more than one non-zero way. 3. Observe that the read result of the read-write conflict contains zero for all ways other than the write way. 4. Observe that reads to this index following the read-write conflict have the correct value. (The problem is only present during write forwarding.) ### Environment - XiangShan branch: master - XiangShan commit id: 977ac3b188267f31bfb32c7fa358f8b923a0e985 - NEMU commit id: N/A - SPIKE commit id: N/A ### Additional context _No response_

Thank you for your report. I can confirm that this is not expected and needs to be fixed. Feel free to submit a fix, as it would be greatly appreciated.

Apologize for the late response.

Also, you may want to checkout these codes.
https://github.com/OpenXiangShan/Utility/blob/6ed7394ef85887ea360f33b3be97bb13fb31e57c/src/main/scala/utility/SRAMTemplate.scala#L301-L358

Okay understood, thanks for the advice. I'm travelling until late next week, I will try to make a fix for it then.

Hello, I'm looking into adding this function to the RAM wrapper now.

The current logic in SC blocks the RAM write during a conflict. However, at least for dual-port RAMs I have used in the past, this would not be necessary. When those RAMs received read and write at the same index, the write would still succeed, but the read result would be corrupt for ways that were written. In this case it is only necessary to bypass the write data, not block the write operation. It is better than the current logic, since the current logic may drop writes when there are back-to-back conflicting reads every cycle.

My question is, what is the required behavior for the dual-port RAM macros? Given that different RAM macros may have different behavior, it is a trade-off between performance and compatibility. I see three possible answers:
1. Simultaneous read and write to same index allowed, but read result is corrupt for ways that were written
2. Simultaneous read and write to same index allowed, but read result is corrupt for all ways
3. Simultaneous read and write to same index not allowed

From a design perspective, I would like to assume (1), since this is best for performance, and RAM macros I used in the past support this. But it would also be possible to make this configurable, in case a future user of XiangShan cannot use RAM macros with this behavior. Please let me know what the preferred choice is for XiangShan. Thanks, Sam

Yes, RAM macros differs among vendors. We've received feedback from a user saying that simultaneous read and write to same index violates their RAM vendor's DRC, which is situation (3) mentioned above. I think it is preferable to have an option for end users to tweak according to their needs.

title: Litex SoC binds to non-existent ports when generating a NaxRiscv-based SoC with --with-jtag-instruction
body:
Hello,

# Issue
I'm trying to implement a NaxRiscv-based SoC on FPGA (Digilent Genesys 2) but synthesis fails, as the SoC's top level module instantiating the Nax tries to connect to port which do not exist.

Precisely, I'm trying to add a JTAG debug module within the Nax, which thus exposes I/O ports in the Nax's top level. For some reason, when integrating the Nax in the SoC's top level, Litex seems to detect different signal names for the JTAG ports, than the ones actually exposed by the Nax, which thus causes an error during synthesis.


Instantation of the NaxRiscv in the SoC top module (namely the verilog file ```build/gateware/digilent_genesys2.v```)
```verilog
//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Instance NaxRiscvLitex_ac66cf5e80a0da4a2f58fc5f9f240934 of NaxRiscvLitex_ac66cf5e80a0da4a2f58fc5f9f240934 Module.
//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
NaxRiscvLitex_ac66cf5e80a0da4a2f58fc5f9f240934 NaxRiscvLitex_ac66cf5e80a0da4a2f58fc5f9f240934(
        /* Remaining ports connections */
        .jtag_instruction_capture           (basesoc_jtag_capture),
        .jtag_instruction_clk               (basesoc_jtag_clk),
        .jtag_instruction_enable            (basesoc_jtag_enable),
        .jtag_instruction_reset             (basesoc_jtag_reset),
        .jtag_instruction_shift             (basesoc_jtag_shift),
        .jtag_instruction_tdi               (basesoc_jtag_tdi),
        .jtag_instruction_update            (basesoc_jtag_update),
        /* Remaining ports connections */
       	);
```

Definition of the NaxRiscv top module
```verilog
module NaxRiscvLitex_ac66cf5e80a0da4a2f58fc5f9f240934 (
	/* Remaining ports declaration */
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_tdi,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_enable,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_capture,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_shift,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_update,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_reset,
	output wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_tdo,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_clk
	/* Remaining ports declaration */
);
	/* RTL */
endmodule
```

As one can see from the above RTL snippets, except for ```jtag_instruction_clk``` which is correct, JTAG signals are declared with prefix ```jtag_instruction_instruction``` whilst the SoC is mapping to ports with prefix ```jtag_instruction```.

# Build options

Here are my build options to try and recreate the issue :
```bash
python3 -m litex_boards.targets.digilent_genesys2.py \
--cpu-type=naxriscv \
--toolchain=vivado \
--build \
--bios-console=lite --bios-format=double \
--synth-mode=vivado \
--bus-standard=wishbone --bus-data-width=32 --bus-address-width=32 --bus-interconnect=crossbar \
--watchdog-width=32 \
--uart-name=serial --uart-baudrate=921600 --uart-fifo-depth=16 \
--l2-size=1024 --integrated-rom-size=131072 --integrated-sram-size=16536 --integrated-main-ram-size=0 \
--sys-clk-freq=200000000.0 \
--no-netlist-cache --update-repo=latest \
--cpu-variant=standard --xlen=32 --cpu-count=1 \
--l2-bytes=131072 --l2-ways=8 --with-rvc --with-fpu --with-coherent-dma \
--with-jtag-instruction
```

Actually, I use a modified version of ```litex_boards.targets.digilent_genesys2``` in which I added  the following lines (right-after the ```BaseSoc``` instantiation in ```main()```) :

```python
from litex.soc.cores.jtag import XilinxJTAG
soc.jtag = jtag = XilinxJTAG(XilinxJTAG.get_primitive(soc.platform.device), chain=4)
soc.comb += [
    soc.cpu.jtag_reset.eq(jtag.reset),
    soc.cpu.jtag_capture.eq(jtag.capture),
    soc.cpu.jtag_shift.eq(jtag.shift),
    soc.cpu.jtag_update.eq(jtag.update),
    soc.cpu.jtag_clk.eq(jtag.tck),
    soc.cpu.jtag_tdi.eq(jtag.tdi),
    soc.cpu.jtag_enable.eq(True),
    jtag.tdo.eq(soc.cpu.jtag_tdo),
]
```

Note: I added the latter modifications following this tutorial from Litex Wiki [JTAG GDB Debugging with VexRiscv SMP NaxRiscv VexiiRiscv CPUs](https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/wiki/JTAG-GDB-Debugging-with-VexRiscv-SMP-NaxRiscv-VexiiRiscv-CPUs#debugging-on-physical-hardware-directly-though-bscane2-jtag-primitive), as I would like to route the JTAG module to the FPGA's built-in JTAG.

# Question

I was wondering if anyone knows why Litex catches wrong names specifically for these signals ? Also, perhaps, is there a way to force the name of these ```XilinxJTAG``` signals to have prefix ```jtag_instruction``` instead of ```jtag_instruction_instruction``` ?

Thanks,
Regards,

#### On the NaxRiscv side

You'll need to modify the file that generates the SoC for Litex, NaxSoc, by changing this line :

https://github.com/SpinalHDL/NaxRiscv/blob/43716b5770e8ac689e9778056c061da577dcf17e/src/main/scala/naxriscv/platform/litex/NaxSoc.scala#L209

by this one : 

```scala
if (withJtagInstruction) debug.instruction.setName("jtag")
```

What happens is that the string `jtag_instruction` is added to the variable name `instruction` in [DebugModuleFiber](https://github.com/SpinalHDL/SpinalHDL/blob/af8fab4da5a73c785c4f2e2f68af2c9b34fd6aec/lib/src/main/scala/spinal/lib/cpu/riscv/debug/DebugModuleFiber.scala#L95) when the verilog is generated.

So to change the name of the totality, another way would be as follows :

```scala
if (withJtagInstruction) debug.instruction.instruction.setName("jtag_instruction")
```

#### On the Litex side

You need to modify the core.py file associated with NaxRiscv.

https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/blob/48e65c199de6bd1d5aead61d7f515356cc7ecab8/litex/soc/cores/cpu/naxriscv/core.py#L428-L437

You need to update the assignments with the “jtag_instruction_instruction” prefix.

```python
self.cpu_params.update(
    i_jtag_instruction_clk     = self.jtag_clk,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_enable  = self.jtag_enable,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_capture = self.jtag_capture,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_shift   = self.jtag_shift,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_update  = self.jtag_update,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_reset   = self.jtag_reset,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_tdi     = self.jtag_tdi,
    o_jtag_instruction_instruction_tdo     = self.jtag_tdo,
)
```

After one of these two modifications, the Vivado synthesis should work.

Best regards

Hello @atkarim,

Thank you for the very quick response.

I tried solution 2, namely bringing changes to the NaxRiscv's ```core.py``` in Litex and now synthesis succeeds. As a consequence, I am closing this issue.

Thanks again,
Best regards,

title: Rocket comes out of reset with valid icache data
body:
Certain randomization values can lead to rocket's icache immediately asserting a valid response. In default rocket-chip configurations this doesn't have any affect on the processor because a debug interrupt comes before the processor is ready to begin executing. But if you were to use a tethered interface to bring up the system there would be no need for the debug interrupt at the start.

My issue then becomes a question:
Should I setup mtvec or similar mechanism before the processor is reset? 
Can I rely on the first instruction at the reset vector to be fetched correctly? 

If this is simply a bug my current fix to this issue for me is the following diff in icache.scala

```
-      val s2_hit = RegEnable(s1_hit, !stall)
+      val s2_hit = RegEnable(s1_hit, Bool(false), !stall)
```

I think @aswaterman would be the best one to answer this question.

comments.body:
I have the same problem.
It seems the requirement failed in pwm.scala:

``` scala
trait PWMTLModule extends Module with HasRegMap {
  val io: PWMTLBundle
  implicit val p: Parameters
  def params: PWMParams

  val w = params.beatBytes * 8
  require(w <= 32)  //FAILED HERE
  ...
}
```

I am new to Scala/Chisel and I can't figure out how does this code work.
It seem that `PWMTLModule` defines an abstract function `params` but not implement it?
And if I assign `w` a fixed number, say, 4, it will compile.
Can anyone give some advices about this problem? 
Thanks a lot!

Sounds like it might be a mismatch between beatBytes coming from rocket-chip and what the PWM module wants.

Are you just using master of this repo?
Yeap, I just using the master branch and its submodules.

I think the problem is that, when XLen is configured as 64-bit, beatBytes equals to 8.
But here w is expected to be smaller than 32, so the requirement failed.
If I modify the code as follows, it will work: 

``` scala
trait PWMTLModule extends HasRegMap {
  val io: PWMTLBundle
  implicit val p: Parameters
  def params: PWMParams

  val w = params.beatBytes * 8
  require(w <= 64)

  // ...
  
  //modify register map to avoid address overlap
  regmap(
    0x00 -> Seq(
      RegField(w, period)),
    0x08 -> Seq(
      RegField(w, duty)),
    0x016 -> Seq(
      RegField(1, enable)))
}
```

Using 64bit register for PWM is waste and totally unneccessary.
but looks like rocketchip have bug regarding using different periphery register width from xbar width.
Sorry I didn't address this issue until now. I'm just going to fix the width at 32 so that we don't have this issue of changing bus widths.

title: Bug report: single-precision multiplication or division followed by conversion sets wrong bits in the mantissa
body:
Hi there!

I've detected a bug in VexRiscv.

## Brief bug description

A single-precision multiplication or division followed by a single-to-double precision conversion may set wrong bits in the mantissa.
This suggests that 5f67075 did not cover all cases. Consequences are likely to be similar to the bugs that 5f67075 intended to fix.

I ran this code on master (b29eb54) where I cherry-picked the fix 5f67075, with the configuration described in #318 .

## Example instance

Here are 2 snippets, one with multiplication and one with division.

### Snippet 1

Here is an example RISC-V (rv32imfd) snippet:
```
  .section ".text.init","ax",@progbits
  .globl _start
  .align 2
_start:
  # Enable the FPU
  li t0, 0x2000
  csrs mstatus, t0
  csrw	fcsr,x0

  la t0, .fdata0
  fld fs1, (t0)

  fmul.s fa5, fs1, fs1
  fcvt.d.s ft7, fa5

  li t0, 0x18
  fsd ft7, 0(t0)

  sw x0, (x0)

infinite_loop:
  jal	x0,infinite_loop

.section ".fdata0","ax",@progbits
  .8byte 0xffffffff1cb31090 # fs1
```

#### Waveform

[Here is a waveform for snippet 1.](https://github.com/SpinalHDL/VexRiscv/files/10888359/fmulfcvt.zip)

#### Expected and actual results

We expect `ft7 = 0x373f500000000000`. I verified this with Spike.
However,  VexRiscv sets additional bits in the mantissa.

### Snippet 2

```
  .section ".text.init","ax",@progbits
  .globl _start
  .align 2
_start:
  # Enable the FPU
  li t0, 0x2000
  csrs mstatus, t0
  csrw	fcsr,x0

  la t0, .fdata0
  fld fa3, (t0)
  la t0, .fdata1
  fld fa4, (t0)

  fdiv.s   ft4,fa3,fa4,rup
  fcvt.d.s fa4, ft4

  li t0, 0x18
  fsd fa4, 0(t0)

  sw x0, (x0)

infinite_loop:
  jal	x0,infinite_loop

.section ".fdata0","ax",@progbits
  .8byte 0xffffffff8002666c # fa3
.section ".fdata1","ax",@progbits
  .8byte 0xffffffff41800000 # fa4
```

#### Expected and actual results

We expect `fa4 = 0xb773330000000000`. I verified this with Spike.
However,  VexRiscv returns `fa4 = 0xb773336000000000` .

Thanks!
Flavien

title: Fix RAS
body:
Currently the RAS is left disconnected, yet some of the logic is synthesized when nRAS > 0.
https://github.com/riscv-boom/riscv-boom/blob/f35cc753a9cc5b15402cf7336f8a98912c6533a3/src/main/scala/bpu/bpd-pipeline.scala#L151-L152

This causes the vestigial RAS to inject false predictions to 0x0 in S1 of BTB, sometimes overriding the valid BTB predictions. In dhrystone MediumBoomConfig with a RAS takes 10% more cycles than SmallBoomConfig with no RAS. Preferably the RAS should be fixed and connected.

Side request: Can we also refactor the RAS to be a module, so that the internal registers and io is available to inspect in waveforms?

fix_commits.messageHeadline: Add verbose to debug runs (#148)

comments.body:
Is the performance bug mentioned above caused by RAS underflow? I just noticed that medium boom uses only 8 entries of RAS and turns off EmptyCheck. Because calling stack of dhrystone is deep, RAS underflow can degrade perfromance significantly.
My result shows that for small boom with 8-entry RAS, EmptyCheck boosts IPC for about 2%.
We found that for programs with a very shallow call stack, the RAS would mispredict more frequently than expected. There is some issue with the RAS update logic which is polluting it.

title: Cache performance will degrade in some simulator due to the implement of module "cache_lru"
body:
Recently I have managed to port the Nyuzi to Xilinx ZC706 evaluation board and run doom & quakeview successfully, with respect. But during this process, I noticed a cache performance degradation when debugging with Modelsim SE 10.5c. Since such degradation seems only existing when simulating in some simulators and doesn't exist in verilator or after synthesize, I think maybe this topic is more like a portability suggestion than an issue.

When running the core on some simulators such as Modelsim, the x value coming from uninitialized SRAM will cause the casez statement in module cache_lru fail to match any pattern, further cause that in all cache set only way 0 is available. To illustrate it clearly, here is a piece of code snipping from cache_lru.sv when parameter NUM_WAYS is 4.

```
...

#130            4:
#131            begin
#132                always_comb
#133                begin
#134                    casez (lru_flags)
#135                        3'b00?: fill_way = 0;
#136                        3'b10?: fill_way = 1;
#137                        3'b?10: fill_way = 2;
#138                        3'b?11: fill_way = 3;
#139                        default: fill_way = '0;
#140                    endcase
#141                end
#142
#143                always_comb
#144                begin
#145                    case (new_mru)
#146                        2'd0: update_flags = {2'b11, lru_flags[0]};
#147                        2'd1: update_flags = {2'b01, lru_flags[0]};
#148                        2'd2: update_flags = {lru_flags[2], 2'b01};
#149                        2'd3: update_flags = {lru_flags[2], 2'b00};
#150                        default: update_flags = '0;
#151                    endcase
#152                end
#153            end

...
```

Consider after reset, two or more cache fill operations happened in the same cache set. When the first fill request comes, because the value of "lru_flags" is 3'bxxx (the value of uninitialized SRAM), the default branch will take effect, way 0 got filled, and the "update_flags" will be 3'b11x. Then, in the subsequent request handling process, the casez statement will always fail to match any pattern with the value of "lru_flags" (3'b11x), the default branch will always take effect, way 0 will always get filled, and "update_flags" will always be 3'b11x. The similar issue also exists when NUM_WAY is 8. The marked red area in the waveform generated by Modelsim attached below shows such situation:

![lru_waveform](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8781507/25722008/1ba40f0e-3145-11e7-93f3-f02092e1a397.png)

Although it sounds like a bad idea, one solution to this problem is changing all casez in cache_lru.sv to casex. I made an experiment to estimate the performance impact: Some logic was inserted into the writeback_stage firstly to trace the function activity. Then, the same program got executed on two different designs, the original design and the design with modified cache_lru, for a given time. Since the program is same, the amount of log generated during simulation is related to the instructions got executed. By comparing the number of function tracing record, we can compare the performance approximately. The screenshot below shows the result: The design with modified cache_lru produced 2.8x more log than the original one, which can roughly be considered as running faster 2.8x.

![log](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8781507/25721242/4dfccdae-3142-11e7-8a54-6c918b5deaa7.png)

The version I use is ce221ff, but this issue still exists in the latest version.

Finally, Thanks for bringing such interesting project!

![img_20170502_233302](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8781507/25722013/219d087a-3145-11e7-8ea3-75685d58b288.jpg)

fix_commits.messageHeadline: Initialize SRAM memories to zero
Fix compilation error w/ Modelsim

comments.body:
Good catch! Nice write up of the issue too, thanks.

Since Verilator is only a two-state simulator (no x or z), it doesn't manifest this problem, but any four-state simulator probably will. Another solution might be to initialize the SRAMs to 0 at startup.
This patch should address the issue, but feel free to let me know if not.

Sadly, if a logic/reg variable is driven in an always_ff block, the "vlog" compiler in the latest Modelsim seems doesn't allow any other block drive that single again, even it's an initial block. So the patch 7780328 just can't pass the compile. 

![compile_error](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8781507/25739227/95386798-31b3-11e7-8bb9-f494bdeacd1e.png)


The following patch is ok with the help of macro SIMULATION, but not very beautiful...

```
--- sram_1r1w_ce221ff.sv        2017-03-23 23:05:54.677195800 +0800
+++ sram_1r1w_patched.sv        2017-05-05 16:32:46.063266600 +0800
@@ -100,7 +100,11 @@
     // Simulation
     logic[DATA_WIDTH - 1:0] data[SIZE];

+`ifdef SIMULATION
+    always @(posedge clk)
+`else
     always_ff @(posedge clk)
+`endif
     begin
         if (write_en)
             data[write_addr] <= write_data;
@@ -120,6 +124,11 @@

     initial
     begin
+`ifdef SIMULATION
+        for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++)
+            data[i] = '0;
+`endif
+
         if ($test$plusargs("dumpmems") != 0)
             $display("sram1r1w %d %d", DATA_WIDTH, SIZE);
     end
```

```
--- sram_2r1w_ce221ff.sv        2017-03-22 23:48:00.614532400 +0800
+++ sram_2r1w_patched.sv        2017-05-05 16:32:48.783422200 +0800
@@ -128,7 +128,11 @@
     // Simulation
     logic[DATA_WIDTH - 1:0] data[SIZE];

+`ifdef SIMULATION
+    always @(posedge clk)
+`else
     always_ff @(posedge clk)
+`endif
     begin
         if (write_en)
             data[write_addr] <= write_data;
@@ -160,6 +164,11 @@

     initial
     begin
+`ifdef SIMULATION
+        for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++)
+            data[i] = '0;
+`endif
+
         if ($test$plusargs("dumpmems") != 0)
             $display("sram2r1w %d %d", DATA_WIDTH, SIZE);
     end
```

Yeah, a bit hacky, but I'm not sure of another way to do this cleanly now. Pushed another patch.

I didn't add the SIMULATION guards in this patch. Did you need that because you are inferring the SRAM for the Xilinx part in that block? I would have expected the last block to not infer SRAMs properly (with an area and clock speed hit), but perhaps this works okay on Xilinx.  It definitely doesn't on Altera. I *think* it might be preferable to have a VENDOR_XILINX block and explicitly instantiate the block RAM, like how it is done in VENDOR_ALTERA, to avoid any issues.

Problem solved with 77a50a8, thanks for the time!

Yes, currently the SRAM in my design is inferred from this block because it just works... Thanks for the advice. I will make a VENDOR_XILINX block and submit a pull request after finished.

title: sequential mtspr calls fail
body:
I have converted to or1k-tests to use inline calls to `mtspr()` and `mfspr()`. This causes failures in the following cases in `or1k-mmu`.

See: https://github.com/openrisc/or1k-tests/commit/32f0ba26bd581ca8cf7d3b4c46a53e2509acdcce

```c
static int itlb_match_test (int way, int set)
{
...

  // Flush these areas incase cache doesn't write them through immediately
  mtspr(OR1K_SPR_DCACHE_DCBFR_ADDR, ta - 8);
  mtspr(OR1K_SPR_DCACHE_DCBFR_ADDR, ta);
(CASE 1 - assembly stores ta to stack at this time)

  mtspr(OR1K_SPR_DCACHE_DCBFR_ADDR, ta + PAGE_SIZE - 8);
  mtspr(OR1K_SPR_DCACHE_DCBFR_ADDR, ta + PAGE_SIZE);

  /* Shifting one in ITLBMR */
  add = (PAGE_SIZE*itlb_sets);
  // Space we'll access and expect the MMU to translate our requests
  ea = add + (set*PAGE_SIZE);

  /* Enable IMMU */
  immu_enable ();

  while (add != 0x00000000) {
(CASE 2)
    mtspr (OR1K_SPR_IMMU_ITLBW_MR_ADDR(way, set), ea | OR1K_SPR_IMMU_ITLBW_MR_V_MASK);
    mtspr (OR1K_SPR_IMMU_ITLBW_TR_ADDR(way, set), ta | ITLB_PR_NOLIMIT);

```
## Case 1 - this happens when 1 nop after mtspr.
The first case is where we have `mtspr` following by a `l.sw`, this causes an invalidate to be sent to the dcache.  At the same time as the write operation.  The write fails.

## Case 2 - this happens with 0 nop after mtspr.
The mtspr followed by mtspr causes the second write to OR1K_SPR_IMMU_ITLBW_TR_ADDR to be lost.

## Workaround
Adding 2 `l.nop`s after `mtspr` fixes the issue.   Below in case 1 the `l.sw` came before the `l.nop` due to some optimizations from gcc, to fix it the `asm` for `l.mtspr` contains the nop inline i.e. `l.mtspr %0, %1, 0; l.nop; l.nop`.  But the below is without the fix exposing the CPU issue, but it should still work.

## Trace case1 - dcache spr mix with l.sw fails

```
    2ff8:       9e b9 20 00     l.addi r21,r25,8192
    2ffc:       aa 20 18 02     l.ori r17,r0,0x1802
    3000:       c0 11 d8 00     l.mtspr r17,r27,0x0  <--- mtspr(OR1K_SPR_DCACHE_DCBFR_ADDR, ta - 8);
    3004:       15 00 00 00     l.nop 0x0
    3008:       c0 11 c8 00     l.mtspr r17,r25,0x0   <--- mtspr(OR1K_SPR_DCACHE_DCBFR_ADDR, ta);
    300c:       d4 01 c8 24     l.sw 36(r1),r25          <--- This store fails to go to dcache (save ta)
    3010:       15 00 00 00     l.nop 0x0
    3014:       c0 11 b8 00     l.mtspr r17,r23,0x0
    3018:       15 00 00 00     l.nop 0x0
    301c:       c0 11 a8 00     l.mtspr r17,r21,0x0
    3020:       15 00 00 00     l.nop 0x0
    3024:       18 80 00 00     l.movhi r4,0x0
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2404255/122664858-d0be2800-d1de-11eb-88fc-a4bf8259eaf3.png)

## Trace case2 - immu spr fails
When we have a l.mtspr writing to the IMMU followed by another l.mtspr writing to the IMMU the second spr write may fail. 

```
    24e0:       aa 94 08 00     l.ori r20,r20,0x800
    24e4:       aa 52 08 00     l.ori r18,r18,0x800
    24e8:       aa 10 03 c0     l.ori r16,r16,0x3c0
    24ec:       9f 51 ff ff     l.addi r26,r17,-1
    24f0:       aa 3e 00 01     l.ori r17,r30,0x1
    24f4:       c0 14 88 00     l.mtspr r20,r17,0x0  <--- This write to IMMUMR goes through
    24f8:       c0 12 80 00     l.mtspr r18,r16,0x0  <--- This write to IMMUTR never happens
    24fc:       d4 02 00 44     l.sw 68(r2),r0
    2500:       d4 02 00 48     l.sw 72(r2),r0
    2504:       d4 02 00 1c     l.sw 28(r2),r0

```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2404255/122664698-f7c82a00-d1dd-11eb-8c52-5f419d56bed9.png)

title: Building cheriot-safe for Artix-A7 100T
body:
Hello,

I have been attempting to build the core for the Arty-A7 100T. I did get it to build but I wanted to point something out and also would like some guidance for getting CHERIot compiled software running on the core.

# Software
I am using Vivado 2022.2

# Commit used
https://github.com/microsoft/cheriot-safe/commit/31ddb4738863aa420e2f95c87ce97b937a3a46e1

# Steps I used to build
1. I created a new project in Vivado targeting the Arty-A7 100T
2. For source directories I added: All directories in 
a. All directories from `src` excluding `msft_cheri_tb`
b. `rtl/` from cheriot-ibex folder
c. `vendor/lowrisc_ip` from cheriot-ibex
3. The top file for me was automatically detected which is: `msftDvIp_cheri_arty7_fpga.sv`
4. I added the constraint file from this reo

# During synthesis and implementatin
When I was synthesising using the Vivado (running as a GUI), I encountered this error: 
```
[Place 30-574] Poor placement for routing between an IO pin and BUFG. If this sub optimal condition is acceptable for this design, you may use the CLOCK_DEDICATED_ROUTE constraint in the .xdc file to demote this message to a WARNING. However, the use of this override is highly discouraged. These examples can be used directly in the .xdc file to override this clock rule.

      < set_property CLOCK_DEDICATED_ROUTE FALSE [get_nets sck0_i_IBUF] >
      sck0_i_IBUF_inst (IBUF.O) is locked to IOB_X1Y114
       and sck0_i_IBUF_BUFG_inst (BUFG.I) is provisionally placed by clockplacer on BUFGCTRL_X0Y31
```
So I added this line to the constraint file in the repo: 
```
set_property CLOCK_DEDICATED_ROUTE FALSE [get_nets sck0_i_IBUF]
```
After adding the line, I managed to build and generate the bitstream.

title: The very first Ethernet frame after reset never leaves the device?
body:
While continuing to investigate network startup time (and https://github.com/FreeRTOS/FreeRTOS-Plus-TCP/issues/1244 in particular), I found what looks like it might be a hardware or driver bug that's beyond my present understanding.  _Specifically, it looks like the Ethernet block fails to send the very first packet it's given._  I am unsure if this is an IP block issue or a driver issue (perhaps we're failing to wait long enough for autonegotiation or link training or somesuch?).  This appears to happen on both warm (`mem_helper.sh`) and cold (power cycle and `mem_helper.sh`) resets of the Sonata.

Turning several debugging knobs up to 11 and adding a few more informative `printf`s, the system spews forth:

* Initialization:
  ```
  Ethernet driver: Acknowledged interrupt, sleeping on futex 0x10bf04 (v:1 0x10bf04-0x10bf08 l:0x4 o:0x0 p: G R----- -- ---)
  vDHCPProcessEndPoint: enter 0
  DHCP-socket[fe-7a]: DHCP Socket Create
  prvCreateDHCPSocket[fe-7a]: open, user count 1
  prvInitialiseDHCP: start after 25 ticks
  vDHCP_RATimerReload: 25
  vDHCPProcessEndPoint: exit 1
  ```

* Attempt to send a DHCP Discover packet without the broadcast-reply flag set (`xUseBroadcast=0`):
  ```
  vDHCPProcessEndPoint: enter 1
  nwf prvSendDHCPDiscover from xHandleWaitingFirstDiscover
  Buffer management: Allocated 0x138 byte buffer: 0x10e630 (v:1 0x10e630-0x10e778 l:0x148 o:0x0 p: G RWcgm- -- ---), descriptor: 0x10e5c8 (v:1 0x10e5c8-0x10e628 l:0x60 o:0x0 p: G RWcgm- -- ---)
  nwf xUseBroadcast=0
  vDHCPProcess: discover
  nwf sendto result 258
  vDHCPProcessEndPoint: exit 2
  Firewall: Permitting broadcast UDP packet
  Firewall: Permitting outbound IPv4 packet
  Ethernet driver: Sending frame of length 0x12c
  Buffer management: Freeing descriptor: 0x10e5c8 (v:1 0x10e5c8-0x10e628 l:0x60 o:0x0 p: G RWcgm- -- ---) and 
  buffer 0x10e630 (v:1 0x10e630-0x10e778 l:0x148 o:0x0 p: G RWcgm- -- ---)
  Ethernet Adaptor: nwf output_frame returning true
  ```

* Timeout, now send a DHCP Discover packet with the broadcast-reply flag set:
  ```
  vDHCPProcessEndPoint: enter 2
  nwf prvSendDHCPDiscover from xHandleWaitingOffer
  Buffer management: Allocated 0x138 byte buffer: 0x10e7e8 (v:1 0x10e7e8-0x10e930 l:0x148 o:0x0 p: G RWcgm- -- ---), descriptor: 0x10e780 (v:1 0x10e780-0x10e7e0 l:0x60 o:0x0 p: G RWcgm- -- ---)
  nwf xUseBroadcast=1
  vDHCPProcess: discover
  nwf sendto result 258
  vDHCPProcess: timeout 1000 ticks
  Firewall: Permitting broadcast UDP packet
  Firewall: Permitting outbound IPv4 packet
  Ethernet driver: Sending frame of length 0x12c
  Buffer management: Freeing descriptor: 0x10e780 (v:1 0x10e780-0x10e7e0 l:0x60 o:0x0 p: G RWcgm- -- ---) and buffer 0x10e7e8 (v:1 0x10e7e8-0x10e930 l:0x148 o:0x0 p: G RWcgm- -- ---)
  Ethernet Adaptor: nwf output_frame returning true
  ```

* _That_ one made it out, and the system gets a reply to it:
  ```
  Ethernet driver: Receiving frame of length 0x15a
  Firewall: DNS server address set to 0x1071dac
  Buffer management: Allocated 0x160 byte buffer: 0x10ea48 (v:1 0x10ea48-0x10ebb8 l:0x170 o:0x0 p: G RWcgm- -- ---), descriptor: 0x10e9e0 (v:1 0x10e9e0-0x10ea40 l:0x60 o:0x0 p: G RWcgm- -- ---)
  Ethernet Adaptor: Sending frame to IP task
  ```

  and so on.

`tcpdump` (no filters beyond the interface, which is set promiscuous) agrees that the first packet it sees from Sonata is a DHCP request _with the broadcast flag set_.  Prior to that, we see the neighbor host doing some MLDv2 announcements as the port comes up.  `3a:30:25:24:fe:7a` is the Sonata; `0c:c4:7a:ab:33:9a` is Sonata's neighbor (bridging Sonata to the larger network); and `b4:fb:e4:20:ca:6b` is the network gateway and DHCP server.


comments.body: On Sonata we connect to an ethernet chip (KSZ8851SNLI-TR) via SPI. We control the SPI host RTL and the Ethernet driver that uses it but we do have to deal with a third-party chip here.

Also, here's the link to the datasheet, which we should probably put on the documentation somewhere: https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/aemDocuments/documents/UNG/ProductDocuments/DataSheets/KSZ8851SNL-Single-Port-Ethernet-Controller-with-SPI-DS00002381C.pdf
Indeed, this looks like a software problem after all: we aren't waiting for linkup before starting the network stack, so that first transmit goes nowhere.
Thanks @nwf for working on this!


PS: I think #109 was supposed to address this, but I do not see how this makes a difference. Example 4-bit timer, max count 15.

* IRQ! We are at count 13. -> We set the next cmp to 4
* Verilog does 13 - 4 = 9, which is greater than zero -> next interrupt fires immediately. 

Without having thought it through, wouldn't the following be the proper fix (and even reduce logic):

* `mtime` always increments 1 (no change)
* if `mtime` == `mtimecmp` -> set IRQ (compare equal, set latching IRQ flag)
* if write to bus -> reset IRQ and update mtimecmp (reset latch on bus access)

OR: As a more extreme alternative, change the timer to a self-resetting kind when it reaches cmp (auto retrigger). Disadvantage: I'll have to check, but we might lose support of tickless kernels, but I'm not sure.

Good debugging! Yes, #109 was supposed to fix this, but in hindsight I should definitely have checked myself that it worked correctly. I don't have any strong opinions on what kind of timer we want to have. The idea was to have a 32-bit timer, but otherwise follow the RISC-V machine timer as closely as possible to make the software support easier. Not sure if I succeeded in that. I agree there's an alarming number of math operations in the IRQ handler, and avoiding those sounds like a good idea. And I'm not sure I understand the implications of a tickless kernel, tbh. Power savings seems to be one thing, but there might be other benefits as well?

A third option could be to just implement a proper 64-bit RISC-V machine timer instead. It will cost a little bit more, but since it's an optional feature outside of the CPU, it's not the end of the world. The 2018 SoftCPU contest is already over by now and that was really the main reason for keeping down the size of the whole SoC.

I can think of a couple of different strategies. One would be to bisect between 2.4 and 3.5 to figure out where it stops working. Or did you say it's not working with 2.4 either? It sucks if we need to wait ten minutes for it to display the problem.

Another way would be to compare the soc support files in serv with the ones upstream and see if there is some issue there.

Replacing the serv_timer with a real risc-v machine timer is probably also a good idea to avoid having to carry our own driver. I started working on that a bit. Will push something later. Also just pushed a branch with some helpful debug registers to make troubleshooting with waveforms slightly less awful https://github.com/olofk/serv/tree/dbg

As noted in PR #111 (https://github.com/olofk/serv/pull/111#issuecomment-1847374609), this problems seems to be related to the toolchain emitting invalid MUL instructions (as part of picolibc, even if disabled), breaking the timing calculations. The driver and Verilog appears to be fine.

title: [BUG] Out-of-Order Not Working
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

## Bug Explanation

I noticed the docs say that Out-of-Order can occur between the multiplier and the ALU, however this is not the case according to the RTL.

Docs:

https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/a29b231070f2dccca53eae2681120116633a4ffc/docs/03_cva6_design/issue_stage.md?plain=1#L42-L54

RTL:

https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/adf99b53042d2b14cbbb36689babf8cd4c03cf81/core/issue_read_operands.sv#L135-L152

For example, I have this code snippet:

```
        div     t2, t0, t1
        fsqrt.s f1, f1
        lw      t5, 0(s1)
        add     t6, t0, t1
```

And this is it's execute stage:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/43790149/223483191-73f6885e-c1e1-4930-bf28-4377288d72b6.png)

As you can see, the `add` instruction isn't run until after the `div` finishes.

## Proposed Fix

Either:

* The RTL could be changed to separate the ALU and multiplier into two separate busy signals.
* The example in the docs could be changed to something else, such as `div` and `lsu`.

comments.body: If you like, I can submit a pull request changing the docs to give div and lsu as the example

Hello @sifferman and thanks for opening this issue.

I had a look, I think I have found a too strict restriction (#1230) related to `mult -> *` sequences. However it does not seem to fix this issue about `div -> flu` sequences.

The parallelism is only possible for units spread on different result buses, so that their result can be provided to the scoreboard without conflicts. For the `div -> add` sequence you show, they use the same result bus (named `flu` as "fixed latency unit", even if div does not have a fixed latency), so you are right, the doc example is wrong.

A few suggestions/ideas:

- We can update the docs as you suggest.
- We could add a write-back port for `mult/div` but we won't as the area cost would be considerable!
- We can check if there is a minimal latency for div; if so, maybe we could issue a few other FLU instructions just after the `div` starts?
- Maybe we could modify how the div result is handled: when div result is available, if result bus is available then push the result, else store it in a (new?) register and lock the `flu` issues until the result bus is available, then release the lock and push the result.
- Maybe we could move the `mult/div` unit to the same port as FP operations?

Thanks for taking a look @cathales! I agree with your observations.

Actually, I believe that the throughput could increase quite a bit if the mult/div unit uses the FP port. On a mult/div instruction, it's probably more likely that the next instruction will be an ALU instruction than a FPU instruction. But I'm not sure how big of an endeavor it would be to complete this.

I will have time to look into it in about a month if progress hasn't been made on it sooner

If we move mult/div to FP port, I hope multiply-accumulate would not need bubbles anymore if the compiler is smart enough to avoid RAW hasards like below:

```asm
mul m0, a, b
; begin repeat
mul m1, a, b ; issue ok
add r, r, m0 ; now: bubble because same bus than previous mul -> after modification: issue ok
mul m0, a, b ; issue ok
add r, r, m1 ; bubble -> issue ok
; end repeat
add r, r, m0 ; issue ok
```

However, if the compiler does not do that (see below), there will be the same bubbles anyway so the modification will not impact performance.

```asm
; begin repeat
mul m, a, b ; issue ok
add r, r, m ; bubble because needs m from mul above and mul duration is 2 cycles
; end repeat
````

> Actually, I believe that the throughput could increase quite a bit if the mult/div unit uses the FP port. On a mult/div instruction, it's probably more likely that the next instruction will be an ALU instruction than a FPU instruction. But I'm not sure how big of an endeavor it would be to complete this.

For CoreMark the increase would be less than 3%, but it depends of the application.

About area:

For a configuration with both F and M, we use an existing write-back port so it is okay.

For a configuration with M, without F, today there should not be a write-back port for FPU, so the muxes in the scoreboard could be cheap. If we add one port for the multiplier, it means that the muxes are big.

So maybe the performance vs area cost should be discussed.

title: StoreQueue cross-16B multi-match partial forward is treated as safe full overlap
body: ### Before start - [x] I have read the [RISC-V ISA Manual](https://github.com/riscv/riscv-isa-manual) and this is not a RISC-V ISA question. 我已经阅读过 RISC-V 指令集手册，这不是一个指令集本身的问题。 - [x] I have read the [XiangShan Documents](https://xiangshan-doc.readthedocs.io/zh_CN/latest). 我已经阅读过香山文档。 - [x] I have searched the previous issues and did not find anything relevant. 我已经搜索过之前的 issue，并没有找到相关的。 - [x] I have reviewed the commit messages from the relevant commit history. 我已经浏览过相关的提交历史和提交信息。 - [x] I have reproduced the incorrect behaviors using the latest commit on the master branch. 我已经使用 master 分支最新的 commit 复现了不正确的行为。 ### Branch kunminghu-v3 ### Describe the bug The StoreQueue forward path can accept a cross-16B partial store-to-load forward as a safe full-overlap forward when the load has multiple matching in-flight stores. The minimal sequence is: ```asm sd zero, 0(t0) sd zero, 8(t0) sd zero, 16(t0) sd zero, 24(t0) fence rw, rw li t1, 0xaabbccdd sw t1, 20(t0) # older store: bytes 20..23 li t2, 0x1122334455667788 sd t2, 12(t0) # younger store: bytes 12..19, crosses the 16B boundary ld a0, 16(t0) # load bytes 16..23 li t3, 0xaabbccdd11223344 bne a0, t3, fail ``` For the `ld a0, 16(t0)`, sequential semantics require: ```text bytes 16..19: from the younger sd 12(t0) = 0x11223344 bytes 20..23: from the older sw 20(t0) = 0xaabbccdd expected a0 = 0xaabbccdd11223344 ``` The reproduced XiangShan run instead writes back: ```text actual a0 = 0x0000000011223344 ``` The target load's memory address is `0x800000d0` (`test_area + 16`). The load instruction PC is `0x80000054`. Affected code path: ```scala // src/main/scala/xiangshan/mem/lsqueue/NewStoreQueue.scala val s2OutMask = ParallelLookUp(s2ByteSelectOffset, s2SelectMask) & s2LoadMaskEnd val s2FullOverlap = (s2SelectDataEntry.byteMask & s2LoadMaskEnd) === s2LoadMaskEnd val s2SafeForward = !s2MultiMatch || s2FullOverlap s2Resp.bits.forwardInvalid := !s2SafeForward || s2Cross4KPage ``` `s2OutMask` is the selected store byte mask after rotation into the load coordinate system. In the failing case it is `0x000f`, so only the low four bytes of the 8-byte load are actually forwarded. However, `s2FullOverlap` compares the unrotated selected-store `byteMask` against `s2LoadMaskEnd`. For this cross-16B case, that unrotated comparison reports full overlap even though the rotated forward mask only covers half of the load. Consequently, `s2SafeForward` is asserted and `forwardInvalid` remains low, so the load is not replayed. The current configuration makes this a real path, not an artificial configuration mismatch: * `XSCoreParameters.VLEN = 128`, so StoreQueue forwarding uses a 16-byte (`VLEN/8`) coordinate. * `SQDataEntryBundle.byteMask` is `(VLEN/8).W`. * `TLMinimalConfig` has `StoreQueueForwardWithMask = true`. * `NewStoreQueue.scala` explicitly handles `cross16Byte`, `s1Next16BMatchVec`, `s2ByteSelectOffset`, and rotated forward data/masks. ### Expected behavior For a multi-match load, if the selected youngest store only covers part of the load after rotation into the load coordinate system, StoreQueue must not treat the forward as safe. It should replay the load or otherwise ensure that all bytes are supplied according to store age order. In this PoC, the expected architectural value for `ld a0, 16(t0)` is: ```text a0 = 0xaabbccdd11223344 ``` StoreQueue should not allow: ```text s2MultiMatch = 1 s2LoadMaskEnd = 0x00ff s2OutMask = 0x000f s2SafeForward = 1 forwardInvalid = 0 ``` because this combination means the load needs 8 bytes, only 4 bytes are forwarded, another matching store exists, and yet the load is allowed to consume the partial result. ### Environment * Software * RISC-V GCC used for the PoC workload: `riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc 15.1.0` * XiangShan checkout HEAD: `3931c5112c528299a23c256bdd77fb90813afa6e` ### To Reproduce The attachment [xiangshan-sq-cross16-forward-poc.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28091274/xiangshan-sq-cross16-forward-poc.zip) contains: 1. `cross16_multistore_forward.S`: minimal bare-metal PoC. 2. `cross16_stale_secret_forward.S`: variant that initializes old memory bytes to `0xdeadbeef` to demonstrate stale-data exposure. 3. `link.ld`: linker script placing `_start` at `0x80000000`. 4. `parse_cross16_vcd.py` and `parse_cross16_secret_vcd.py`: VCD monitors for the main and stale-data variants. 5. `monitor_repro_0_11550.json` and `monitor_secret_0_11700.json`: reproduced monitor results. 6. `cross16_repro_hier_16740_16770.{vcd,fst}` and `cross16_secret_hier_16738_16768.{vcd,fst}`: small hierarchy-preserving waveforms containing the relevant SQ/writeback signals around the failing event. 7. `run_repro_0_11550.log` and `run_secret_0_11700.log`: emulator logs. Build the main PoC: ```bash riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc \ -nostdlib -nostartfiles \ -march=rv64gc_zicsr_zifencei -mabi=lp64 \ -T link.ld \ -o cross16_multistore_forward.elf \ cross16_multistore_forward.S riscv64-unknown-elf-objcopy \ -O binary \ cross16_multistore_forward.elf \ cross16_multistore_forward.bin riscv64-unknown-elf-objdump \ -dr cross16_multistore_forward.elf \ > cross16_multistore_forward.objdump ``` Run the waveform-enabled XiangShan emulator: ```bash emu \ -C 11550 -b 0 -e 11550 \ -i cross16_multistore_forward.bin \ --no-diff \ --dump-wave-full \ --wave-path=cross16_repro_0_11550.vcd \ --force-dump-result \ > run_repro_0_11550.log 2>&1 ``` Parse the VCD: ```bash python3 parse_cross16_vcd.py \ cross16_repro_0_11550.vcd \ --json-out monitor_repro_0_11550.json \ > monitor_repro_0_11550.log 2>&1 ``` The reproduced result is: ```text predicate_result = reproduced expected_load_data = 0xaabbccdd11223344 bad_writebacks = 0x0000000011223344, 0x0000000011223344 good_writebacks = [] ``` At VCD time `16758`, the StoreQueue monitor sees: ```text s2Valid = 1 s2Resp_valid = 1 s2ForwardValid = 1 s2MultiMatch = 1 s2LoadMaskEnd = 0x00ff s2OutMask = 0x000f s2SafeForward = 1 forwardInvalid = 0 s2LoadPaddr = 0x800000d s2LoadStart = 0 ``` At VCD time `16760`, integer writeback port 0 writes: ```text toIntRf_valid = 1 toIntRf_bits_isFromLoadUnit = 1 toIntRf_bits_pdest = 0x0f toIntRf_bits_data = 0x0000000011223344 toRob_bits_debugInfo_vaddr = 0x800000d0 toRob_bits_debugInfo_paddr = 0x800000d0 ``` This connects the StoreQueue partial-forward decision to an architectural integer-register writeback for the target load. ### Additional context The stale-data variant changes only the initial bytes at `test_area + 16` before the older `sw`: ```asm li t4, 0xdeadbeefcafebabe sd t4, 16(t0) ... sw t1, 20(t0) sd t2, 12(t0) ld a0, 16(t0) ``` Sequential semantics still require: ```text a0 = 0xaabbccdd11223344 ``` The reproduced stale-data variant instead writes back: ```text a0 = 0xdeadbeef11223344 ``` The stale high 32 bits should have been overwritten by the older `sw 20(t0)`. This shows that the bug can expose stale bytes architecturally when software relies on an in-flight store to overwrite previous memory contents. This is not a branch-prediction or Spectre-style transient-execution issue. It is an out-of-order load/store forwarding correctness bug in the speculative memory-execution machinery. The incorrect value is not merely transient; it reaches integer-register writeback and changes the architectural path (`bne a0, t3, fail`). In principle, Spike/NEMU difftest should also catch this: Spike executes the sequence sequentially and obtains `a0 = 0xaabbccdd11223344`, while the reproduced XiangShan run writes `a0 = 0x0000000011223344`. In this workspace, the available `build_vcd/emu` was used with `--no-diff` for waveform evidence; passing `--diff` to this particular binary prints the help text and exits, so I used VCD-based validation instead.

For people like me looking for a solution to the problem, an easy solution is to edit `micropython/ports/litex/Makefile` :

```
$(Q)$(CC) $(LDFLAGS) -o $@ $^ $(LIBS)
```

to be replaced with

```mk
$(Q)$(CC) $(LDFLAGS) -march=rv32i -o $@ $^ $(LIBS)
```

The reason is that `newlib` in my toolchain only supports the following targets:

```bash
$ ls /usr/lib/gcc/riscv64-elf/12.2.0/rv*
rv32i/      rv32im/     rv32imafc/  rv64imafdc/ 
rv32iac/    rv32imac/   rv64imac/
```
but as suarezvictor says it is set to `-march=rv32i2p0`.

Also, if you need LTO, replace it with:

```
$(Q)$(CC) $(LDFLAGS) -march=rv32i -misa-spec=2.2 -o $@ $^ $(LIBS)
```

title: PTW incorrectly marks the access fault type for out-of-range non-leaf PTEs
body:
<!-- THIS REPOSITORY'S ISSUES ARE RESERVED FOR FEATURE REQUESTS AND BUG REPORTS. -->
<!-- For support questions related to Rocket Chip, please use [Stack Overflow [rocket-chip]](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/rocket-chip). -->
<!-- For support questions related to Chisel, please use [Stack Overflow [chisel]](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/chisel). -->
<!-- Please select the item best describing the issue in each category and delete the other items. -->

<!-- choose all that apply -->
**Type of issue**: bug report

<!-- choose one -->
**Impact**: unknown

<!-- choose one -->
**Development Phase**: proposal

**Other information**
 <!-- include detailed explanation, stacktraces, related issues, suggestions how to fix, links for us to have context, eg. Stack Overflow, gitter, etc -->

**If the current behavior is a bug, please provide the steps to reproduce the problem:**
In S mode, the PTW gets a valid, non-leaf PTE with a PPN exceeding the physical address space.

**What is the current behavior?**
Rocket-chip checks the PPNs (`!invalid_paddr` in PTW.scala:316) before traversing to the next level of page table. It thens returns `ae_final` to the TLB. However, since the page is non-leaf, it does not have the `r` bit set. Therefore, further a read request to TLB is responded with a page-fault exception.

**What is the expected behavior?**
According to the RISC-V manual 5.3.2, in step 4, if the PTE is valid and `pte.r = 0` and `pte.x = 0`, the PTE is a pointer to the next level of page table. Since we have not finished the three levels of page table, we continue to step 2 and `a = pte.ppn X PAGESIZE` to calculate the base address. If accessing the PTE violates the PMA, it should raise an access-fault exception.

This is the same behavior as in Spike. As seen in `mmu_t::walk`, if the PTE points to the next level of page table and does not have any bits of `PTE_D | PTE_A | PTE_U | PTE_N | PTE_PBMT` set, then we calculate the next base address with `base = ppn << PGSHIFT;` and continue to the next iteration of the for loop. In the next level, if accessing the PTE violates PMA (like exceeding the physical address space), an access-fault exception is raised.


**Please tell us about your environment:**
<!--    (examples)
    - version: `git commit hash`
    - OS: `Linux knight 4.4.0-92-generic #115-Ubuntu SMP Thu Aug 10 09:04:33 UTC 2017 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux`
-->
Found during co-simulating rocket-chip with riscv-isa-sim. Page-fault is delegated so rocket-chip goes to S mode while the Spike goes to M mode because of access-fault.
```
   mode different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x0000000000000003, wrong = 0x0000000000000001
mstatus different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x8000000a000060a2, wrong = 0x8000000a000060a8
sstatus different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x8000000200006022, wrong = 0x8000000200006020
   mepc different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x0000000000011186, wrong = 0x000000000001116e
   sepc different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x0000000000010a1a, wrong = 0x0000000000011186
  mtval different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x0000003f9bdf749e, wrong = 0x0000000000000000
  stval different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x0000003f9c07ffac, wrong = 0x0000003f9bdf749e
 mcause different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x0000000000000005, wrong = 0x0000000000000002
 scause different at pc = 0x0000011184, right= 0x000000000000000f, wrong = 0x000000000000000d
```

**What is the use case for changing the behavior?**
Just to align the behavior with Spike and the ISA. I don't think it would be a serious issue for users.

I notice the `pte_addr` is shortened after traversing to the next level. So I think it would be a little bit complicate to fix the behavior by allowing it traverse to the next level. Probably we should just set `ae_ptw` instead in this case.

PTW: set ae_ptw instead ae_final for non-leaf PTEs
PTW: set ae_ptw for out-of-range non-leaf PTEs
PTW: fix the condition for reserved, non-leaf PTEs

comments.body:
I tried a fix. This time rocket-chip raises the same access-fault as riscv-isa-sim does.

```
diff --git a/src/main/scala/rocket/PTW.scala b/src/main/scala/rocket/PTW.scala
index 7c36bdbf3..1e0930b77 100644
--- a/src/main/scala/rocket/PTW.scala
+++ b/src/main/scala/rocket/PTW.scala
@@ -720,7 +720,8 @@ class PTW(n: Int)(implicit edge: TLEdgeOut, p: Parameters) extends CoreModule()(
           resp_valid(r_req_dest) := true.B
         }
 
-        resp_ae_final := ae
+        resp_ae_ptw := ae && count <= 1.U && !pte.r && !pte.x
+        resp_ae_final := ae && (count > 1.U || pte.r || pte.x)
         resp_pf := pf && !stage2
         resp_gf := gf || (pf && stage2)
         resp_hr := !stage2 || (!pf && !gf && pte.ur())
```

Please correct me if I'm wrong. If the bug is confirmed, I can submit a PR to fix it.

Probably I'm still missing the condition of reserved bits. Only if the non-leaf PTEs are valid and its PPN refers to an invalid address should we raise access-fault, because accessing the next-level PTE would violate the PMA.

Besides, I found that there may be a separate bug in the page-fault condition in PTW. Currently it checks only the most significant reserved bits (`val pf = pte.v && pte.reserved_for_future =/= 0.U`). However, as discussed in https://github.com/riscv-software-src/riscv-tests/issues/352, non-leaf should not have any of D, A, and U bits set. Therefore, rocket-chip needs to check the D, A, U bits as well for page-fault.

I believe rocket-chip's page-fault condition then would become exactly the same as Spike:
```
if (pte & (PTE_D | PTE_A | PTE_U | PTE_N | PTE_PBMT))
  break;
```

So there would be two separate bugs, for page-fault and access-fault respectively.

The missing cases are:
- access-fault: (1) it is a valid non-leaf PTE; (2) its PPN refers to an invalid address.
- page-fault: a non-leaf PTE has any of D, A, and U bits set.

I've updated two commits to fix the two issues respectively.

- access-fault for non-leaf out-of-range PTE access: https://github.com/poemonsense/rocket-chip/commit/ff025a69dbc9b230de9a2ad386c9b333a92ea46c
```diff
diff --git a/src/main/scala/rocket/PTW.scala b/src/main/scala/rocket/PTW.scala
index 7c36bdbf3..8701caa0b 100644
--- a/src/main/scala/rocket/PTW.scala
+++ b/src/main/scala/rocket/PTW.scala
@@ -720,6 +720,7 @@ class PTW(n: Int)(implicit edge: TLEdgeOut, p: Parameters) extends CoreModule()(
           resp_valid(r_req_dest) := true.B
         }
 
+        resp_ae_ptw := ae && count < (pgLevels-1).U && pte.table()
         resp_ae_final := ae
         resp_pf := pf && !stage2
         resp_gf := gf || (pf && stage2)
```
For non-leaf PTEs (`pte.table()` is set, and `count` is less than the `pgLevels`), we should set `resp_ae_ptw` instead of `resp_ae_final`. Besides, since `resp_ae_final` would have lower priority than page-fault and `ae_ptw` access-fault, we don't need to shrink its condition and keep the condition as simple as possible. 

- page-fault for reserved, non-leaf PTEs: https://github.com/poemonsense/rocket-chip/commit/2a005655d2487fdb0da4e7a526abfff348d2aecb
```diff
diff --git a/src/main/scala/rocket/PTW.scala b/src/main/scala/rocket/PTW.scala
index 8701caa0b..be45281f7 100644
--- a/src/main/scala/rocket/PTW.scala
+++ b/src/main/scala/rocket/PTW.scala
@@ -135,8 +135,12 @@ class PTE(implicit p: Parameters) extends CoreBundle()(p) {
   val r = Bool()
   /** valid bit */
   val v = Bool()
+  /** the most significant bits are reserved for all types of PTE */
+  def isReserved: Bool = reserved_for_future =/= 0.U
+  /** a non-leaf PTE has more reserved bits than the leaf PTEs */
+  def nonLeafIsReserved: Bool = d || a || u
   /** return true if find a pointer to next level page table */
-  def table(dummy: Int = 0) = v && !r && !w && !x && !d && !a && !u && reserved_for_future === 0.U
+  def table(dummy: Int = 0) = v && !r && !w && !x && !isReserved && !nonLeafIsReserved
   /** return true if find a leaf PTE */
   def leaf(dummy: Int = 0) = v && (r || (x && !w)) && a
   /** user read */
@@ -695,7 +699,7 @@ class PTW(n: Int)(implicit edge: TLEdgeOut, p: Parameters) extends CoreModule()(
     }.otherwise {
       val gf = stage2 && !stage2_final && !pte.ur()
       val ae = pte.v && invalid_paddr
-      val pf = pte.v && pte.reserved_for_future =/= 0.U
+      val pf = pte.v && (pte.isReserved || count < (pgLevels-1).U && !pte.leaf() && pte.nonLeafIsReserved)
       val success = pte.v && !ae && !pf && !gf
 
       when (do_both_stages && !stage2_final && success) {
```
I notice that, `table()` already has the correct checker logic for a valid non-leaf PTE in the bundle. Therefore, I just split the conditions and raise page-fault if any of the reserved bits for non-leaf PTEs is set.

Do you think these two bugs and fixes make sense? Notice that you added the valid `table()` condition for non-leaf PTEs. @aswaterman

Thank you very much for bug reports, pull requests for fixes, and thorough descriptions; all excellent!  Much appreciated.

This will be closed by https://github.com/chipsalliance/rocket-chip/pull/3407.  For others, see that PR, and https://github.com/chipsalliance/rocket-chip/pull/3408, for discussion that we have already had on each.
